prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing the measurement of time to unprecedented precision and accuracy

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B029) because I put the discovery in nature first, but after reading the opening ballots I move to optical lattice clocks (B041) as my preferred configuration. Six of eight members rank it in their top three, including two first places, and every proposer names the same pair, Katori and Ye. The physics is clean and the attribution is unusually well defined: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light-shift problem and made many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free spectroscopy possible, while Ye's group brought stability and accuracy to the 1e-18 level and used the clocks for real measurements, such as relativistic redshift across millimetres, tests of constants and searches for new physics. It is mature, reproduced in many laboratories and compared across continents, and the redefinition of the second is a live prospect. It also sits close to the committee's tradition of rewarding precision tools that open new measurements. I accept that this is an invention and a measurement capability more than a discovery of a new object, which is the point where I still feel the pull of B029, but the instrument-to-discovery chain here is already visible in its uses.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a clock is a capability rather than a discovery of something unexpected in nature. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) cover frequency combs and single-ion control, so the marginal step must be argued as the many-atom lattice regime and not as precision spectroscopy in general. The credit is clean for the named pair, but groups at SYRTE, PTB, NIST and elsewhere made substantial contributions, and a pair necessarily leaves them out. If the committee wants a discovery about the universe rather than a tool, B029 or B017 is the better answer.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first, as I did, as a new observational window that addresses the origin of cosmic rays, and notes that the diffuse flux is confirmed while the TXS 0506+056 association rests on a modest chance-coincidence significance. He does not think Yoshida is decisive and prefers Halzen and Karle.
responses.response: I agree on the pair, and on the maturity point I think your own caveat cuts deeper than either of us stated: the diffuse flux is secure, but the source identifications rest on one blazar at about three sigma and on NGC 1068, which is a small sample. That makes a citation to 'the discovery of astrophysical neutrinos' safe but 'neutrino astronomy' ahead of the evidence, and it also leaves open that KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD will sharpen the picture within a few years. That is why I moved IceCube to my first alternative and not my preferred prize this year. I would still defend it if the committee wants a discovery first.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first and IceCube fourth, and says the physical results of IceCube are less deep than the instrument, and that a large collaboration makes any three-person credit arbitrary.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and it contributed to my move away from B029: there is no principled way to cut a 300-plus collaboration at two or three names, and Halzen as conceiver and Karle as builder are a judgement, not a measurement. I disagree that the physical result is shallow, since a diffuse flux at PeV energies is a fact about nature that no theory predicted in detail. On your own first choice, B003 has only your ranking behind it, and the credited set (Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks, Seifert) shows its own boundary problem, with the early Evans-Cohen-Morriss work, the Jarzynski equality and the Crooks theorem each a separate step. I would want the citation for that to be explicit about which result is being honoured before I could support it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first with Katori and Ye, stresses 1e-18 uncertainty and the role of Ye's many-body clock work, and ranks the Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion proposals second and IceCube last because the individual credit is loose.
responses.response: I agree with the clock assessment and rely on your point that independent clocks agree below 1e-18, which settles maturity. Where I differ is on IceCube: loose individual credit is a problem for the citation but does not lower the scientific importance, so I would not push it to the bottom. On Cirac and Zoller, which I ranked fourth and you ranked second, I accept the pair is clean, but our shared reservation is that experimental realisation was largely honoured in 2012, so the prize would be for theory whose computing promise is not yet delivered.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first as the cleanest case where what can be measured has changed, notes that other groups (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley) contributed, and says the next superconducting-circuit award should wait after 2025.
responses.response: I share your view that clocks are the cleanest case, and I agree the omission of Lemonde, Gill and the NIST and PTB teams has to be acknowledged in the citation by tying it to the invention and the record performance, not to every clock. On circuit QED I agree with your timing concern and add that the three-person cap forces a choice between Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff that I cannot make convincingly, so I rank it low, which is why I do not list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks altermagnetism first and magic-angle graphene fifth, finding the graphene interpretation not stable enough and the recognition somewhat early.
responses.response: I partly share your reservation on B017: the existence of the correlated phases is well reproduced, but the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, which is why it is my second alternative and not my preferred prize. I disagree that this makes the flat-band prediction and its confirmation premature, because a clean prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by an experimental discovery in 2018 is the structure the prize rewards. Altermagnetism is attractive as a symmetry-based classification, but with one first-place vote and no other member ranking it, I think it needs more time and independent device-level evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a measurement-capability invention such as optical lattice clocks as ahead of a discovery in nature such as IceCube, given prior prizes in precision spectroscopy in 2005 and 2012.
How to divide credit for IceCube among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and the wider collaboration; I cannot verify individual contributions from the supplied text.
Whether the origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene will be settled enough to make B017 mature.
Whether the SI redefinition of the second, if it occurs soon, would strengthen or only confirm the case for B041.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot.
